newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Socialists, Communists agree poll strategy.
newsitem.headline: French Socialists, Communists agree poll strategy.

text.p: The heads of France's Socialist and Communist parties, uneasy allies when not outright enemies for nearly 80 years, agreed a joint strategy on Tuesday which skirted their differences over Europe ahead of a snap election.

Both Socialist Lionel Jospin and Communist Robert Hue had insisted they would aim solely to define goals rather than reach an official pact to govern together in case of victory in the May 25-June 1 parliamentary poll.
"We wanted to commit ourselves clearly against the right. We want to prepare the change we believe the French want," Jospin told a news conference after the two reached agreement in talks.
"We propose to unite to create not a fragile France but one of solidarity. This is not a common programme nor an agreement about government," said Hue, briefing reporters separately.

The programme called for a cut in the work week to 35 hours from 39 with no loss in salary, rejected any further budget austerity, urged efforts to create 700,000 youth jobs, and pledged a halt to privatisations including Air France and France Telecom.
The parties did not attempt to resolve their differences over a planned single European currency, which the Socialists conditionally support and the Communists oppose.

"We do not want to hide our differences. Each is presenting his own programme and his own identity to the electorate," Hue said, adding that the two parties would propose talks with other European Union countries on giving social issues more weight within the 15-nation bloc.
The Jospin-Hue meeting began under uncertain auspices after a first gathering of nearly all the left-wing groups earlier in the day attended by Socialists, Communists and smaller leftist movements.
That earlier meeting was to agree on single candidates for the first round of voting in constituencies where the extreme rightist National Front (FN) was expected to score heavily.
Participants said no agreement had been reached because the Communists told those present that they would not sign any agreement on the issue.

Jospin, whose party is forecast by most opinion polls to win about 220 seats compared with only 25 or so for the Communists in the 577-seat National Assembly, had levelled a warning to Hue even before they met.
"The Communist Party must ask itself questions about its historical future, about its identity and about its position," he told an election rally late on Monday.
"The Soviet Union has disappeared and the movement which began in 1917 ended the way we know in 1989. That means all those who were involved in that must ask themselves real questions," Jospin said.
His strong words were apparently aimed at countering warnings by centre-right politicians of the "Red menace" which a Socialist-Communist government might portend for France.
The French Communist Party was long one of the most pro-Soviet in Europe, run on strict Stalinist lines.
The well-informed daily newspaper Le Monde said on Tuesday that the document the two sides would sign made no mention of the Communists participating in a future cabinet.
Hue said on Monday that if the Communists participated in a cabinet, "it would show that the left has remained to the left".
